name: Venezuela
summary_text: Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents. Caracas has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.

sources.title: LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after disputed election
sources.claim_summary: Washington Blade (Sep 2024): 'LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after disputed election' — post-election crackdowns ensnare LGBTQ people; detention and abuse reported.

sources.title: 3.5. LGBTIQ+ | European Union Agency for Asylum
sources.claim_summary: EUAA Venezuela Country Focus, section 3.5 'LGBTIQ+ persons': country-of-origin assessment of the situation of LGBTIQ+ persons in Venezuela.
NOTE: The AFS/Vance Center LGBTQ guide on Venezuela (Oct 2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

sources.title: Venezuela's first transgender candidate Tamara Adrian to run for Congress
sources.claim_summary: SMH/Reuters (Aug 2015): Venezuela's first transgender candidate, Tamara Adrian, registered for Congress under her given male name (Thomas) because Venezuelan law does not allow legal gender change despite her 2002 surgery; she argued Venezuela, with Paraguay, Guyana, Suriname and Peru, has done little for equal rights.

sources.title: Mayoría de venezolanos apoya derechos para comunidad LGBTIQ
sources.claim_summary: Crónica Uno (March 2023, in Spanish): an Equilibrium Cende survey found 76% of Venezuelans support LGBTIQ people being honest about their sexual orientation and gender identity - majority public support for equal rights.

Sabina Becker blog (Jan 2014): 'Equal marriage: coming soon to Venezuela?' - the sex/gender diversity community presented the egalitarian civil-marriage bill to modify Article 44 of the Civil Code; recalls the TSJ's 2008 Sentence 190 that the constitution does not discriminate on sexual orientation.

sources.claim_summary: El Mundo (Dec 2015, in Spanish): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla - deputy-elect and openly gay activist of Voluntad Popular, founder of Proinclusión which first requested same-sex marriage in the National Assembly - a prisoner of conscience, held in Sebin; he became the first openly gay parliamentarian in Venezuela's history.
